common_name: Mediopicta Aurea Century Plant (Gold-Striped Variegated Agave)

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; the broad golden-yellow center band is the reverse pattern of the older, more common Mediopicta Alba selection and bleaches less in hot, bright exposure.

directions: Site in full sun with lean, mineral, sharply drained soil, since rich or constantly moist ground encourages rot and dulls the variegation. Mediopicta Aurea is a striking sport of the common century plant, each broad gray-green leaf stamped down its center with a wide, irregular band of rich golden-yellow rather than the white of the older Mediopicta Alba form, giving established rosettes a glowing, sunlit appearance even in shade. It keeps the same massive, imposing proportions and dangerously spined leaf margins as the species, so site it well away from paths and play areas and expect it to eventually flower once and die after many years, leaving offsets behind. Because variegated sports rarely come true from seed, propagate only from basal offsets to maintain the golden pattern.

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this Texas native agave is sold under both Agave univittata and its accepted synonym Agave lophantha, so labels vary by nursery.

directions: Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; this compact rosette-forming selection layers four colors into each narrow leaf — a creamy-yellow margin, a thin red line, a dark green band, and a pale central stripe — making it one of the most vividly patterned small agaves in general cultivation. It offsets readily, forming a tight clump within a few seasons that can be divided to propagate true-to-type plants rather than relying on seed, which does not reliably reproduce the variegation. The toothed, reddish-brown marginal spines are showy but sharp, so give it clearance from foot traffic. It tolerates brief light freezes better than many tropical agaves but still benefits from winter protection at the colder edge of its range.

common_name: Shira Ito No Ohi Thread-Leaf Agave (White-Threaded Japanese Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in gritty, mineral, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; this Japanese-selected clone is prized among collectors for unusually dense, bright white marginal curling filaments.

directions: Grow in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun for the tightest rosette and whitest filament display; too much shade loosens the form and dulls the thread color. This selection of the thread-leaf agave produces an exceptionally dense covering of curling white fibers peeling from the narrow leaf margins, set off by dark, glossy green blades arranged in a tight, symmetrical spiral. It stays small and slow-growing, making it well suited to container culture, rock gardens, and collector display among other miniature agaves. Offsets form slowly at the base and can be separated once they have their own roots to increase named stock.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; protect from frost, since variegated tissue is more cold-sensitive than the solid green species.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in bright light; strong light keeps the creamy-yellow leaf margins vivid, while deep shade causes the variegation to fade toward solid green over time. This spineless, soft-leaved sport of the popular foxtail agave forms the same broad, arching, trunk-topping rosette as the species but with each wide blue-green leaf bordered in a bold cream-to-yellow band. It offsets steadily to form handsome clumps and lacks the sharp spines of most agaves, making it comfortable to plant near walkways and seating areas in frost-free gardens. Grow it in a container where winters bring hard freezes, since it is among the more cold-tender agaves in general cultivation.

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in gritty, mineral, sharply drained soil in full sun; this slow-growing Coahuila species is often still sold under its older synonym Agave ferdinandi-regis.

directions: Plant in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; this slow-growing Mexican limestone native forms an extremely symmetrical, nearly spherical rosette of broad, dark green, spineless-margined leaves etched with narrow white leaf-bud imprint lines, closely resembling its relative Agave victoriae-reginae but with proportionally wider leaves and a flatter overall profile. It is solitary for most of its long life, rarely producing offsets, so most nursery stock is grown from seed or tissue culture rather than division. Despite coming from a limited native range, it tolerates real winter cold once established as long as drainage stays sharp and the crown is kept dry through the dormant season.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; protect from hard freezes, since this coastal Oaxacan species is one of the more cold-tender large landscape agaves.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this native of the limestone hill of Cerro Guiengola in coastal Oaxaca forms a broad, open rosette of smooth, pale blue-gray leaves with widely spaced marginal teeth and a relatively short terminal spine compared with similarly large agave species. It offsets moderately to form handsome colonies over time and is valued in warm xeriscape gardens for its large scale and cool silvery color, which pairs well with darker-leaved companion succulents. Because it comes from a frost-free coastal climate, it needs winter protection or container culture outside the mildest regions.

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; the broad, glossy leaves and bold reddish-brown teeth make this one of the showiest medium agaves from the Sierra Madre Occidental foothills.

directions: Plant in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; native to pine-oak foothill canyons of Sonora and Chihuahua, this species forms a broad rosette of wide, glossy, bright green leaves edged with large, closely spaced, curved reddish-brown teeth resembling the horns that give it its common name. It grows faster than many ornamental agaves and tolerates light afternoon shade better than most desert species, reflecting its origin in a slightly moister, higher-rainfall habitat than the true Sonoran Desert. Give it winter protection or a container at the colder edge of its range, since it is less cold-hardy than high-elevation agaves such as Agave parryi.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Garland's Gold Yucca (Compact Gold-Margined Weak-Leaf Yucca)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions or pups in spring in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun; this compact, award-winning selection stays smaller and more garden-scaled than straight species yucca.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun to light shade. Garland's Gold forms a compact, outward-arching rosette of soft-tipped, blue-green leaves broadly edged in a bright golden-yellow band that deepens in color through the cooler months and intensifies with stronger light exposure. Like other weak-leaf yuccas its foliage lacks a dangerous spine, making it a safer choice than stiff-leaved species near paths and patios, while still sending up tall summer spikes of nodding, creamy-white, bell-shaped flowers. It is extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established and slowly forms offsets at the base that can be divided to propagate new, true-to-type plants.

common_name: Bright Star Yucca (Gold-Centered Variegated Mound Lily Yucca)

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this variegated selection of mound lily yucca is slower and more compact than plain green Yucca gloriosa.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun for the strongest coloration, since shade mutes the variegation and encourages looser, floppier growth. Bright Star carries a broad golden-yellow stripe through the center of each stiff, blue-green leaf, a bolder and more consistently golden effect than most variegated mound lily selections, which more commonly show cream or white margins. It builds the same architectural, eventually trunk-forming rosette as the species, though more slowly, and sends up tall late-summer flower spikes of large, bell-shaped, creamy-white blooms. Remove spent flower stalks after bloom and give it sharp drainage, especially through winter, to prevent crown rot.

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; site away from paths and play areas, since the rigid leaf tips are needle-sharp like the straight species.

directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun; this long-cultivated variegated form of Spanish bayonet bears stiff, dagger-like leaves edged in creamy white that often flush soft pink in cool weather and strong light, a more colorful counterpart to the plain green species. Over years it slowly develops the same woody, sometimes branching trunk as straight Yucca aloifolia, eventually reaching small-tree proportions in favorable climates. Its rigid, needle-tipped leaves are strikingly ornamental but genuinely hazardous, so give it generous clearance from walkways, seating, and areas used by children or pets. It tolerates salt spray and sandy coastal soils as well as the species does, making it a long-standing choice for seaside landscaping.

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; site away from paths, since the rigid leaf tips are needle-sharp like the straight species.

directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun. Marginata is an old garden selection of Spanish bayonet with each stiff, blue-green, dagger-shaped leaf bordered in a narrow golden-yellow band, giving established clumps a warmer, more colorful presence than the plain species while keeping the same rigid, architectural form. Like the species it slowly develops a woody trunk and can eventually branch into a small, multi-headed tree in frost-free climates, with tall late-season spikes of creamy-white, bell-shaped flowers. The stiff, needle-tipped leaves are hazardous, so plant it with generous clearance from walkways and play areas, and expect excellent tolerance of salt spray, wind, and sandy coastal soils.

common_name: Tricolor Spanish Bayonet (Pink-Blushed Striped Aloe Yucca)

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets in spring in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; site away from paths, since the rigid leaf tips are needle-sharp like the straight species.

directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun for the strongest color development. Tricolor layers three tones into each stiff, dagger-shaped leaf — a pale creamy-yellow stripe, a dark green band, and a pink-tinged edge that deepens in cool weather — making it one of the most colorful forms of Spanish bayonet in cultivation. It shares the species' eventual woody, sometimes branching trunk and tall late-season spikes of creamy-white flowers, growing slowly into small-tree proportions in frost-free gardens. The rigid, needle-tipped leaves are genuinely dangerous, so give it clearance from walkways and areas used by children or pets, and expect the same excellent salt and wind tolerance that makes Spanish bayonet a long-standing coastal landscape plant.
